tool.name: ASP.NET Core
tool.tagline: Microsoft's framework for building web APIs and web apps in C#
tool.description: ASP.NET Core is the part of .NET for building web servers in C#: web APIs that apps call, websites and live-updating services. It comes with everything a server needs built in — matching requests to code, settings, logging, sign-in and a fast web server called Kestrel — and runs on Windows, macOS and Linux. It is a top choice for company back ends and cloud services.

glossary.def: The web server built into ASP.NET Core: the part that listens for HTTP requests and hands them to your app.
The part of an app that creates your registered services and hands them to whatever needs them, deciding how long each instance lives.
ASP.NET Core's lightweight style of building web APIs: you connect each URL and HTTP method straight to a lambda or method, with no controller classes.
A method's name used on its own, without calling it, so it can be passed where a delegate or lambda is expected.
A URL pattern such as /todos/{id} that says which request paths an endpoint matches; the parts in braces are filled in from the path.
A named placeholder in a route template, like {id} in /todos/{id}, whose value is taken from the request's path.
A rule on a route parameter, like {id:int}, that the value must satisfy for the route to match at all.
A set of endpoints that share a path prefix and settings, such as authorization rules, created with MapGroup.
A standard JSON or YAML description of a web API's endpoints, inputs and responses, which tools use to draw documentation pages and generate client code.
How long one instance of a registered service lives: the whole app (singleton), one request (scoped) or one use (transient).
A short-lived service trapped inside a long-lived one: for example a per-request service held by a singleton, so it is never replaced.
One source of settings for an ASP.NET Core app, such as appsettings.json, environment variables or the command line.
A .NET tool that keeps development passwords and keys in a private file on your own machine, outside the project folder, so they never end up with the code.
Reading a section of settings into a plain C# class and receiving it through dependency injection as IOptions<T>, instead of looking up text keys.
Model–View–Controller: the classic way to organise ASP.NET Core apps, where requests are handled by methods on controller classes.
In ASP.NET Core, a class whose methods (called actions) each handle requests for one endpoint, in the MVC style.
A public method on a controller that handles requests for one endpoint and returns the response.
Attributes such as [Required] and [Range] that state the rules a property's value must follow, so the framework can check input for you.
EF Core's main class: one session with the database that tracks the objects you load and writes your changes back.
A generated file describing one change to a database's structure, such as adding a table or column, that a tool can apply to the database.
A standard JSON shape for error responses, with fields such as title, status and detail, so callers can read every error the same way.
A log message with named placeholders, like "Order {OrderId} shipped", whose values are kept as separate data so log tools can search and filter on them.
How important a log message is, from Trace and Debug up to Warning, Error and Critical; settings choose the lowest level that gets written.
Logging where each message carries named values as separate data, not just text, so you can search and count by those values.
A web page that shows an OpenAPI description as interactive documentation, where you can try each endpoint from the browser.
A test helper that starts your real ASP.NET Core app inside the test process, so tests can send it requests without a network.
An access token sent in the header Authorization: Bearer <token>. Whoever holds (bears) it is treated as the user it was issued to, so it must be kept secret.
One statement about a signed-in user, such as their id, email or role, carried inside a token or cookie.
One way an ASP.NET Core app can identify callers, such as checking a bearer token or reading a sign-in cookie.
A named set of access rules, such as 'must have the admin role', that endpoints refer to instead of repeating checks.
A class the app starts alongside the web server and keeps running in the background for the app's whole life, for jobs like working through a queue.
A lock shared by several copies of an app, usually kept in a database or Redis, so only one copy does a job at a time.
Code that runs just before and after one minimal API handler, with access to its parameters, to check or change the input or result.
Saving whole HTTP responses on the server and sending the saved copy for repeat requests, instead of running the handler again.
Many requests missing the cache for the same item at once and all rebuilding it together, overloading the database behind it.
Headers a proxy adds to tell the app who the original caller was (their IP address) and whether they used HTTPS.
When all thread-pool threads are stuck waiting, so new work queues up and response times jump even though the processor is idle.
The .NET service that creates HttpClient objects for outgoing requests, reusing connections safely and adding features such as automatic retries.
One timed step inside a trace, such as handling a request or calling the database, with its start time, duration and details.
An open standard and set of libraries for collecting traces, metrics and logs from programs and sending them to monitoring tools.
The OpenTelemetry protocol: the standard format for sending traces, metrics and logs from an app to a monitoring service.
A system that runs containers across many machines, restarts them when they fail, and starts or stops copies to match the load.
In web security, a string a server or sign-in service hands out, which the caller sends with later requests to prove who it is, like a ticket.

concepts.name: How the web works: requests and responses
concepts.summary: Before writing a server: how a client and a server talk over HTTP with requests, responses, URLs, status codes and JSON.
concepts.why: Everything ASP.NET Core does is about receiving one kind of message and sending back another; this lesson names the parts.
concepts.body:
Every time you open a website, or an app on your phone loads fresh data, two programs are talking. The one asking — your **browser**, or the app — is the **client**.

The program answering, on another computer, is the **server**. **ASP.NET Core** is Microsoft's toolkit for writing servers in C#.

They talk using **HTTP**, an agreed set of rules for the messages they exchange.

The client's message is a **request**; the server sends back exactly one **response**. One question, one answer — and the next request starts afresh.

A request says where it is going with a **URL**, a web address such as `https://shop.example.com/products/42?color=red`. After the site's name comes the path (`/products/42`), naming what you want, and an optional **query string** (`?color=red`) with extra details as `name=value` pairs.

A request also has an **HTTP method**, a verb saying what to do:

- `GET` — fetch something (opening a page is a `GET`).
- `POST` — send something new, such as a filled-in form.
- `PUT` or `PATCH` — change something; `DELETE` — remove it.

Requests and responses carry **headers**: labelled extra details such as `Content-Type: application/json`, saying what kind of data is attached. Many also carry the data itself — a submitted form, say, travels in the **request body**.

Every response starts with a **status code**, a three-digit number saying how it went: `200` OK, `201` created, `400` your request was wrong, `404` not found, `500` the server broke. The first digit gives the family: 2xx success, 4xx the client's mistake, 5xx the server's fault.

**Web pages** — what a browser shows — are written in **HTML**. But when programs talk to each other, the data is usually **JSON**, a text format of names and values: `{"id": 42, "name": "Lamp"}`.

Programs offer each other operations through an **API** (application programming interface): a menu of things you can ask for, and how to ask. A **web API** is one you call over HTTP, usually exchanging JSON.

Each method-and-path a web API answers, like `GET /products/42`, is one **endpoint**. Most of this course is about building web APIs with ASP.NET Core.
concepts.code:
# curl is a command-line tool that sends one request and prints the response.
# -i shows the status line and headers too.
curl -i "https://api.github.com/repos/dotnet/aspnetcore"

# HTTP/2 200                                   <- status code: OK
# content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8  <- a header
#
# {                                            <- the body, in JSON
#   "id": 17620347,
#   "name": "aspnetcore",
#   "language": "C#",
#   ...
# }

# Another request: the GET method spelled out, plus a query string (?q=...):
curl -i -X GET "https://api.github.com/search/repositories?q=aspnetcore"
takeaways: A client sends a request; the server sends back exactly one response
A request has a method (`GET`, `POST`...), a URL, headers and maybe a body
Status codes: 2xx success, 4xx the client's mistake, 5xx the server's fault
Web APIs exchange JSON; each method plus path is an endpoint
pitfalls: Thinking the server remembers earlier requests by itself — each request arrives on its own, with everything the server needs to answer it.

quiz.q: An app asks for a product that doesn't exist. Which status code fits the response?
quiz.explain: 4xx codes mean the request can't be satisfied as asked; 404 specifically means not found.

quiz.q: In https://shop.example.com/search?term=lamp&page=2, what is the query string?
quiz.explain: The query string is the part after the ?, holding name=value pairs.

concepts.name: Your first ASP.NET Core app
concepts.summary: Create an app with dotnet new web, understand Program.cs — the builder and the app — and run it on the built-in Kestrel server.
concepts.why: Every ASP.NET Core service starts from this same small Program.cs structure.
concepts.body:
Create an app from the terminal with `dotnet new web -o Api`, which makes an almost empty project, then start it with `dotnet run`. While you work, `dotnet watch` applies your changes whenever you save, without a manual restart — **hot reload**.

The app listens on an address from `Properties/launchSettings.json`, such as `http://localhost:5000`. **localhost** is your computer's name for itself, and 5000 is the **port**: a numbered door, so one machine can run many servers side by side. Open that address in a browser and you'll see the response.

`Program.cs` has two phases. **Build**: `var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);` gathers settings (from `appsettings.json`, **environment variables** — named settings handed to a program when it starts — and the command line). It also sets up the **DI container**, the dependency injection system that creates your services. You register services on `builder.Services`.

**Run**: `var app = builder.Build();` creates the app. You then add **middleware** — code that every request passes through, added with `app.UseX()` — and endpoints (`app.MapGet(...)`). Finally `app.Run()` starts the server and keeps it running until you stop it.

The server inside is **Kestrel**, a fast server for HTTP that ships with ASP.NET Core and runs on Windows, macOS and Linux. On a live server it can face the internet directly, or sit behind a **reverse proxy**: a front server, such as Nginx, that receives requests first and passes them on.

The project file uses the `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web` SDK, which already includes what ASP.NET Core needs: no extra packages for matching requests to endpoints, JSON, dependency injection, settings or **logging** (writing notes about what the app is doing).

The **environment** setting, `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT`, is usually `Development` on your machine and `Production` on the live server real users rely on (**production**). It changes behaviour such as detailed error pages and which settings file is loaded; check it with `app.Environment.IsDevelopment()`.
takeaways: CreateBuilder sets up settings, logging and the DI container; Build creates the app
Register services before Build; add middleware and endpoints after
Kestrel is the server built into ASP.NET Core
ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT switches between Development and Production behaviour
pitfalls: Trying to register services on builder.Services after builder.Build() has been called.

quiz.q: Where do you register a service class that your endpoints depend on?
quiz.explain: The DI container is built by builder.Build(), so registrations must happen before it.

concepts.name: Routing and minimal API endpoints
concepts.summary: Connect HTTP methods and paths to handler code with MapGet, MapPost and friends, using route parameters and checks like {id:int}.
concepts.why: Routes are the public face of your API; designing and matching them correctly is step one.
concepts.body:
**Minimal APIs** connect a **route template** (a path with placeholders, such as `/todos/{id}`) and an HTTP method directly to a handler, usually a lambda. Choosing which handler runs for an incoming request is called **routing**:

```csharp
app.MapGet("/todos/{id}", (int id) => ...);
```

There is one method per HTTP method: `MapGet`, `MapPost`, `MapPut`, `MapPatch`, `MapDelete`, plus `MapMethods` for others. The handler can also be a **method group** — just a method's name, like `Handlers.GetX` — which keeps `Program.cs` short as the app grows.

Route templates:

- `{id}` is a **route parameter**: it captures one segment of the path (the part between two slashes), and a handler parameter with the same name receives it, converted to its type. If the value can't be converted, the response is a 400 and the handler isn't called.
- **Route constraints** restrict what matches: `{id:int}`, `{slug:alpha}`, `{n:min(1)}`, `{code:length(3)}`, `{date:datetime}`. With one in place, `/todos/abc` doesn't match at all (404), so another route can take it.
- Optional `{id?}`, defaults `{page=1}`, and catch-all `{*path}` for the rest of the path.

Routing picks the **most specific** matching endpoint, whatever order you declared them in: a fixed segment like `/todos/today` beats `/todos/{id}`. If two endpoints match equally well, the request fails with an exception.

Name endpoints with `.WithName("GetTodo")` so you can generate links to them, and use **route groups** (`app.MapGroup("/todos")`, covered later) to share prefixes and settings. Keep handlers thin: they should read the input, call a service and shape the response.
takeaways: MapGet/MapPost/... connect an HTTP method and a route template to a handler
{name} segments bind to the handler parameter with the same name
Route constraints like {id:int} make non-matching URLs fall through to 404
The most specific route wins, not the first declared
pitfalls: Relying on declaration order to pick between overlapping routes; ASP.NET Core ranks by specificity instead.

quiz.q: With routes /items/{id:int} and no other match, what does GET /items/abc return?
quiz.explain: The int constraint prevents the route from matching, so no endpoint is found.

concepts.name: Binding request data
concepts.summary: Get route values, query strings, headers, JSON bodies and services into handler parameters.
concepts.why: Correct binding gives you typed, checked input instead of digging through the request by hand.
concepts.body:
Minimal API handlers declare what they need as parameters, and ASP.NET Core **binds** each one: it fills the parameter in from the request. The rules, roughly in order:

- Explicit attributes win: `[FromRoute]`, `[FromQuery]`, `[FromHeader(Name = "X-Api-Key")]`, `[FromBody]`, `[FromForm]`, `[FromServices]`.
- Special types are passed in directly: `HttpContext` (everything about the current request), `HttpRequest`, `HttpResponse`, a **CancellationToken** that fires when the caller disconnects, so you can stop work early, and `ClaimsPrincipal` (the signed-in user, covered later).
- A parameter whose name matches a route parameter binds from the route.
- Simple types (`int`, `string`, `Guid`, `DateTime`, **enums**, anything with a `TryParse` method) otherwise bind from the query string. Arrays like `int[] ids` bind from repeated keys: `?ids=1&ids=2`.
- Types registered in the DI container come from there.
- Any other type is read from the JSON request body with `System.Text.Json`, which expects names in camelCase (`firstName`) by default. Only one body parameter is allowed.

Nullability matters: `string? q` or a default value (`int page = 1`) makes a query parameter optional; a non-nullable one that is missing produces a **400**.

`[AsParameters]` groups many parameters into one record or class, keeping handler signatures tidy.

Records are a natural fit for request bodies: `record CreateTodo(string Title, DateOnly? Due);`. Don't bind straight to the classes you save in your **database** (the app's permanent store of data); use separate request types, so callers can't set properties like `Id` or `IsAdmin`.
takeaways: Route names bind from the route, simple types from the query string, other types from the JSON body
Nullable or defaulted parameters are optional; missing required ones give 400
Use [FromHeader], [FromQuery] etc. to be explicit
Bind to request records, not the classes you store in the database
pitfalls: Declaring two complex-type parameters and expecting both to come from the body.

quiz.q: For app.MapGet("/items", (int page) => ...), what does GET /items (no query string) return?
options: The handler runs with page = null
quiz.explain: page is a required non-nullable parameter, so missing input fails binding with 400.

concepts.name: Responses and status codes
concepts.summary: Return JSON, status codes and headers using plain objects, Results and TypedResults.
concepts.why: Callers depend on correct status codes and response shapes; together they are your API's contract.
concepts.body:
What a handler returns becomes the response:

- A `string` is sent as **plain text** (`text/plain`) with 200.
- Any other object (record, list, anonymous type) is converted to JSON — **serialized** — and sent with 200.
- An `IResult` takes full control: status code, headers and body.

The `Results` and `TypedResults` static classes create IResults: `Ok(value)`, `Created(uri, value)`, `NoContent()`, `BadRequest(error)`, `NotFound()`, `Conflict()`, `Problem(...)`, `ValidationProblem(errors)`, `Unauthorized()`, `Forbid()`, `Redirect(url)`, `File(bytes, contentType)`, `Stream(...)`, `StatusCode(429)`.

Prefer **TypedResults**: they return specific types like `Ok<Todo>`, so the handler's return type documents its possible outcomes, and **OpenAPI** — a standard description of your API that tools read (a later lesson) — can list them automatically. When a handler has several outcomes, declare them all in its return type:

```csharp
static Results<Ok<Todo>, NotFound> Get(int id) => ...
```

Each branch returns a different TypedResult, and the compiler checks that only the declared ones are used.

Async handlers return `Task<T>` and work the same way. Use status codes that say what happened: 201 with a `Location` header (where the new item can be found) when you create something, 204 for a successful delete with no body, 404 when the item doesn't exist, 400 or 422 for invalid input, and 409 for a conflict such as a duplicate.

JSON options — how names are written, or sending **enums** (types with a fixed set of named values) as their names — are set with `builder.Services.ConfigureHttpJsonOptions(o => ...)`.
takeaways: Objects become JSON, strings become plain text
Return an IResult to choose the status code and headers
TypedResults + Results<A, B> make the possible outcomes explicit
Use the right status code for each outcome

quiz.q: Why prefer TypedResults.Ok(todo) over Results.Ok(todo)?
options: Its concrete return type documents the outcome for the compiler and OpenAPI
quiz.explain: TypedResults return specific types such as Ok<Todo>, which tools can read to describe the response.

concepts.name: Dependency injection
concepts.summary: Register services with singleton, scoped and transient lifetimes and receive them in handlers and constructors.
concepts.why: Dependency injection is the backbone of every ASP.NET Core app: data access, outgoing HTTP calls, logging and your own services all flow through it.
concepts.body:
ASP.NET Core has a built-in DI container. You register services on `builder.Services` — typically an interface plus the class that implements it — and ASP.NET Core creates them and passes them wherever they're needed: endpoint handler parameters, constructors, middleware and other services.

Each registration has a **service lifetime**, saying how long one instance lives:

**Singleton** (`AddSingleton`) — a **singleton** is one instance for the whole app, used by many requests at the same moment. It must therefore be **thread-safe**: safe to use from several threads at once. Good for **caches** (stores of saved results to reuse), settings wrappers and clocks.

**Scoped** (`AddScoped`) — one instance per HTTP request, shared by everything that handles that request. The usual choice for code that talks to a **database** (the app's permanent store of data).

**Transient** (`AddTransient`) — a new instance every time one is needed. For small services that keep no data between uses.

The DI container fills in constructor parameters automatically, so a service can depend on other services, which depend on others in turn. Prefer receiving dependencies through the constructor; avoid asking `IServiceProvider.GetService` for them yourself, which hides what a class needs.

The classic mistake is a **captive dependency**: a singleton that takes a scoped service in its constructor keeps that one instance forever, sharing it across all requests. In Development the DI container checks for this and throws at startup.

Other features: `TryAdd*` avoids registering the same service twice; **keyed services** register several implementations under names (`AddKeyedSingleton<IStore, S3Store>("s3")`, received with `[FromKeyedServices("s3")]`); and libraries offer `AddX()` methods that register all their services in one call.
takeaways: Register on builder.Services; the container creates and passes in instances
Singleton = whole app, Scoped = one request, Transient = every time one is needed
Never inject scoped services into singletons (captive dependency)
Prefer receiving services through the constructor over asking IServiceProvider yourself
pitfalls: Registering a database-access service as a singleton, so one instance that isn't thread-safe is shared by every request.

quiz.q: A singleton service takes a scoped service in its constructor. What's the problem?
options: None, the container creates a new scoped instance per call
The scoped instance is captured and lives as long as the singleton
quiz.explain: The singleton is created once, so it holds the first scoped instance forever: a captive dependency.

concepts.name: Configuration and options
concepts.summary: Read settings from appsettings.json, environment variables and user secrets, and bind them to typed options classes.
concepts.why: Every app needs different settings in different places without code changes — and passwords must never be saved with the code.
concepts.body:
`WebApplication.CreateBuilder` loads settings from several **configuration providers** (sources), and later ones override earlier ones:

1. `appsettings.json`
2. `appsettings.{Environment}.json` (e.g. `appsettings.Development.json`)
3. **User secrets** — a private settings store on your own machine, for development only (`dotnet user-secrets set "Db:Password" "x"`)
4. Environment variables
5. Arguments typed after `dotnet run`

Keys are nested with `:` separators (`ConnectionStrings:Main`). In environment variable names use a double underscore instead: `Smtp__Host=mail.local` sets `Smtp:Host`. Hosting platforms let you set environment variables, so this is how you configure an app on a live server.

Read values directly with `builder.Configuration["Smtp:Host"]` or `GetConnectionString("Main")`, but prefer the **options pattern**: a plain class filled in from one section of the settings.

```csharp
builder.Services.Configure<SmtpOptions>(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Smtp"));
```

Then inject `IOptions<SmtpOptions>` (read once, singleton), `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` (re-read per request, scoped) or `IOptionsMonitor<T>` (updates live when the settings change).

Check options at startup so bad settings fail fast: `AddOptions<SmtpOptions>().BindConfiguration("Smtp").ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart();`.

Never put **secrets** — passwords, keys — in appsettings.json, which is saved with your code. Use user secrets locally, and environment variables or a **secrets manager** such as Azure Key Vault in production.
takeaways: Later sources override earlier ones: JSON, environment JSON, user secrets, environment variables, command line
Use __ in environment variable names for nested keys
Bind sections to classes with the options pattern
Check options on start; keep secrets out of your code

quiz.q: Which environment variable sets the configuration key Logging:LogLevel:Default?
quiz.explain: A double underscore stands in for the : separator in environment variable names.

concepts.name: The middleware pipeline
concepts.summary: See how requests flow through ordered middleware, write your own middleware, and place the built-in ones correctly.
concepts.why: Error handling, security checks and serving files are all middleware, and putting them in the wrong order causes subtle mistakes.
takeaways: Middleware runs in the order added, then in reverse on the way out
Call next to continue; skip it to answer early
Exception handler first; authentication before authorization
Headers can't change after the response has started
pitfalls: Adding UseAuthorization before UseAuthentication, so the caller is never identified when the access rules run.

quiz.q: Why is UseExceptionHandler usually registered first?
options: It is required to be first by the compiler
It can only catch exceptions thrown by middleware registered after it
quiz.explain: Middleware wraps the components added after it, so the earliest one sees all later exceptions.

concepts.name: MVC controllers for APIs
concepts.summary: Build APIs with [ApiController] classes, attribute routing, ActionResult<T> and automatic input checks.
concepts.why: Many existing codebases and teams use controllers instead of minimal APIs; you need to read and write both styles.
concepts.body:
**Controllers** are the classic alternative to minimal APIs, from the **MVC** (Model–View–Controller) style of ASP.NET Core. A controller is a class that derives from `ControllerBase`, with **action methods** — one per endpoint — connected to routes by attributes:

```csharp
[ApiController]
[Route("api/[controller]")]
public class TodosController(ITodoStore store) : ControllerBase
```

- `[HttpGet("{id}")]`, `[HttpPost]`, `[HttpPut]`, `[HttpDelete]` connect actions to routes; `[controller]` is replaced by the class name without the `Controller` suffix.
- Return `ActionResult<T>`: either a `T` (serialized with 200) or a helper result like `NotFound()`, `CreatedAtAction(...)` or `NoContent()`.
- Dependencies arrive through the constructor (a primary constructor keeps it short).

`[ApiController]` adds conventions. Complex parameters bind from the body without `[FromBody]`. And input that breaks the rules — a bad JSON body, or a property failing a **DataAnnotations** attribute such as `[Required]` or `[Range]` — automatically gets a **400** with a **problem details** body listing the errors, before the action runs.

Register with `builder.Services.AddControllers()` and `app.MapControllers()`. Controllers and minimal APIs can live side by side in one app.

Which to choose? Minimal APIs are leaner, start faster and can be compiled ahead of time for very fast startup (Native AOT, an Expert lesson). Controllers offer a structured convention with filters, custom binding and an organisation large teams know. New projects increasingly use minimal APIs organised with route groups, but the ideas — routing, binding, results, dependency injection — are the same.
takeaways: Controllers derive from ControllerBase and use attribute routing
ActionResult<T> returns either a T or a status result
[ApiController] binds complex types from the body and returns 400 on invalid input
AddControllers + MapControllers wire them up

quiz.q: What does [ApiController] do when a required property is missing from the JSON body?
options: Returns 400 with validation problem details before the action runs
quiz.explain: Automatic input checks stop invalid requests with a 400 problem details response before the action runs.

concepts.name: Data access with EF Core
concepts.summary: Map C# classes to database tables with EF Core: DbContext, migrations, LINQ queries and saving changes.
concepts.why: EF Core is the default way .NET services talk to relational databases — databases that store data in tables of rows and columns.
concepts.body:
**Entity Framework Core** (EF Core) is .NET's **ORM** (object-relational mapper): you describe your data as C# classes, and EF Core turns your LINQ queries into **SQL**, the language databases understand, and writes your changes back.

- Install a provider package for your database, e.g. `Npgsql.EntityFrameworkCore.PostgreSQL` or `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite`.
- Create a **DbContext** class with a `DbSet<T>` property per table.
- Register it: `builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDb>(o => o.UseNpgsql(connString))`. Contexts are **scoped** — one per request — and not thread-safe.

**Migrations** change the database's structure (its **schema**: tables and columns) to match your classes. `dotnet ef migrations add Initial` generates C# code from your model changes; `dotnet ef database update` applies it. For production, prefer generating a SQL file that is safe to run more than once: `dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent`.

Queries use LINQ on `IQueryable`, which is turned into SQL only when you ask for results with `ToListAsync`, `FirstOrDefaultAsync` or `CountAsync`. Write filters and `Select` projections **before** that call, so the database does the work and sends back only the columns you need. `AsNoTracking()` speeds up read-only queries.

Saving: add, change or remove tracked objects, then `await db.SaveChangesAsync()`, which runs all the changes in one **transaction** — they succeed or fail together. For bulk updates without loading objects first, use `ExecuteUpdateAsync` / `ExecuteDeleteAsync`.

Load related data explicitly with `Include(o => o.Items)`. Automatic loading of related data on first use is off by default, which avoids the hidden "N+1" problem: one query for a list, then one more per item.
takeaways: DbContext + DbSet<T> describe the database; register it scoped with AddDbContext
Migrations generate and apply changes to the database structure
Filter and project before ToListAsync so the work happens in SQL
SaveChangesAsync writes tracked changes in one transaction
pitfalls: Calling ToList() early and filtering in memory, loading whole tables.

quiz.q: Why must a DbContext not be registered as a singleton?
options: It can't be constructed by DI
It would use a different database
It isn't thread-safe and its change tracker would grow across all requests
quiz.explain: A DbContext is a short-lived unit of work; sharing one across concurrent requests corrupts its state.

concepts.name: Validation and error handling
concepts.summary: Check input with DataAnnotations, and return consistent problem details for errors and exceptions.
concepts.why: Callers need predictable error responses, and unexpected exceptions must never leak internal details.
concepts.body:
**Validation** — checking input before using it. ASP.NET Core 10 adds built-in validation for minimal APIs: call `builder.Services.AddValidation()` and mark request types with DataAnnotations (`[Required]`, `[Range]`, `[StringLength]`, `[EmailAddress]`, `[RegularExpression]`). Invalid input gets a **400** whose body lists the errors per property, before your handler runs. Controllers with `[ApiController]` have done this for a long time. For complex rules, implement `IValidatableObject` or use a library such as FluentValidation.

**Problem details** (RFC 9457) is the standard JSON shape for errors: `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance`, plus your own extra fields. `builder.Services.AddProblemDetails()` makes ASP.NET Core use it for its error responses, and `TypedResults.Problem(...)` / `ValidationProblem(...)` let you return it yourself.

**Exceptions.** Add `app.UseExceptionHandler()` early in the pipeline, so unhandled exceptions become a 500 problem response instead of a raw stack trace. In Development, a detailed developer error page is shown instead. To turn specific exceptions into specific status codes, implement `IExceptionHandler` and register it with `AddExceptionHandler<T>()`; return `true` from `TryHandleAsync` when you've written the response.

`app.UseStatusCodePages()` adds bodies to empty 4xx/5xx responses (such as a 404 from routing).

Throwing exceptions for expected outcomes (not found, invalid input) is slow and hides the flow of your code; return results for those, and keep exceptions for the unexpected.
takeaways: AddValidation + DataAnnotations check minimal API input automatically (.NET 10)
Problem details is the standard shape for error bodies; turn it on with AddProblemDetails
UseExceptionHandler turns unhandled exceptions into safe 500 responses
Return results for expected failures; keep exceptions exceptional
pitfalls: Sending exception messages or stack traces to callers in production.

quiz.q: What does UseExceptionHandler with AddProblemDetails return for an unhandled exception in Production?
options: A 500 response with a generic problem details body
quiz.explain: It catches the exception and writes a generic 500 problem details response without internal details.

concepts.name: Logging
concepts.summary: Write structured logs with ILogger<T>, message templates and log levels, and configure them per category.
concepts.why: Logs are your main window into what a live app is doing, and into what went wrong.
concepts.body:
ASP.NET Core ships with `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging`. Inject `ILogger<T>` — its **category** is the type's name — and call `LogInformation`, `LogWarning`, `LogError` and friends.

Use **message templates**, not string interpolation:

```csharp
logger.LogInformation("Order {OrderId} shipped to {City}", order.Id, city);
```

The named placeholders become separate values attached to the log entry — **structured logging**. Log storage services (Seq, Elasticsearch, Application Insights, OpenTelemetry) can then filter and count by them. Interpolation would bake the values into one-off text, and would do that formatting work even when the message is switched off.

**Log levels**, from lowest to highest: `Trace`, `Debug`, `Information`, `Warning`, `Error`, `Critical`. Set the minimum level per category in configuration:

```json
"Logging": { "LogLevel": { "Default": "Information", "Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning" } }
```

Pass exceptions as the first argument: `logger.LogError(ex, "Payment {Id} failed", id)` keeps the stack trace as structured data.

`logger.BeginScope("Request {RequestId}", id)`, used in a `using` block, attaches values to every log entry written inside that block.

In code that runs extremely often, the `[LoggerMessage]` attribute makes the compiler generate a dedicated, strongly typed logging method that avoids creating temporary objects.

Built-in providers write to the console and debugger output. Libraries like Serilog or the OpenTelemetry exporter plug into the same `ILogger` interface, so your code doesn't change when the destination does. Never log passwords, access tokens or full personal data.
takeaways: Inject ILogger<T>; the type becomes the category
Use message templates with named placeholders, not interpolation
Set minimum log levels per category in Logging:LogLevel
Pass the exception as the first argument to LogError
pitfalls: Writing logger.LogInformation($"User {id}"), which loses the separate values and always formats the text.

quiz.q: Why prefer logger.LogInformation("User {Id}", id) over $"User {id}"?
options: Interpolated strings are not allowed in logs
Id is kept as a separate value and no formatting happens when the level is switched off
quiz.explain: Message templates keep values as structured data and avoid formatting work for disabled levels.

concepts.name: OpenAPI documents
concepts.summary: Generate an OpenAPI description of your API with Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi and enrich it with endpoint details.
concepts.why: An OpenAPI document powers interactive documentation, generated client code and automatic checks for breaking changes.
concepts.body:
ASP.NET Core can describe its endpoints as an **OpenAPI** document: a JSON file listing every endpoint, its inputs and its responses. Since .NET 9 this is built in through the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi` package (included in the `webapi` project template); the older Swashbuckle package is no longer part of the template.

```csharp
builder.Services.AddOpenApi();
app.MapOpenApi();        // serves /openapi/v1.json
```

In ASP.NET Core 10 the document uses **OpenAPI 3.1** by default, and you can also serve it as **YAML**, a more readable text format (`app.MapOpenApi("/openapi/{documentName}.yaml")`).

The generator reads what it can from your code: routes, parameter types and where they bind from, request bodies, and response types from `TypedResults` and `Results<...>` return types. Add more with methods on the endpoint:

- `.WithName("GetTodo")` (the operation's id), `.WithSummary(...)`, `.WithDescription(...)`, `.WithTags("Todos")`.
- `.Produces<T>(201)`, `.ProducesProblem(404)` when the return type doesn't say it.
- XML documentation comments (`/// <summary>`) are picked up when `GenerateDocumentationFile` is on (ASP.NET Core 10).
- Document and operation **transformers** customise the output, e.g. to describe how callers sign in.

The package only produces the document. For an interactive page, add **Swagger UI** (`Swashbuckle.AspNetCore.SwaggerUI`) or Scalar (`Scalar.AspNetCore`) pointing at it, usually only in Development.

Treat the document as a contract: generate typed client code from it (NSwag, Kiota, openapi-generator), and compare it with the previous version in your automated builds to catch **breaking changes** — changes that would stop existing callers from working.
takeaways: AddOpenApi + MapOpenApi serve /openapi/v1.json
TypedResults and Results<...> document responses automatically
Add names, summaries and tags with With* methods
Interactive pages like Swagger UI or Scalar are separate add-ons

quiz.q: Why do TypedResults help OpenAPI generation?
options: Their static types describe the possible responses and schemas
They are required for any document
quiz.explain: The generator inspects the declared return types, such as Results<Ok<Todo>, NotFound>, to list responses.

concepts.name: Integration testing with WebApplicationFactory
concepts.summary: Test the whole request pipeline in memory with WebApplicationFactory, HttpClient and replaced services.
concepts.why: Integration tests — tests of several parts working together — catch routing, binding, DI and JSON mistakes that unit tests miss.
concepts.body:
`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing` provides **WebApplicationFactory**`<TEntryPoint>`, which starts your real app (its `Program`) on an **in-memory** test server inside the test process. `factory.CreateClient()` returns an `HttpClient` connected to it: requests go through the full middleware pipeline, routing, binding and JSON conversion, without opening a network port.

Setup:

- Create an xUnit project, add `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing`, and reference the web project.
- The test project needs access to `Program`. If the compiler can't see it, add `public partial class Program { }` at the end of the app's `Program.cs`.
- Use `IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>` to share one app instance across the tests in a class.

Customise the app for tests with `WithWebHostBuilder`:

- `builder.UseEnvironment("Testing")` and `UseSetting("Key", "value")` for settings.
- `ConfigureTestServices(services => ...)` to replace real dependencies (outside APIs, clocks, email senders) with fakes. Remove the real registration, or rely on the last registration winning.

For databases, prefer a real database engine — started in a throwaway container by Testcontainers — or SQLite, over EF Core's in-memory provider, which doesn't behave like a real relational database.

Use the `System.Net.Http.Json` helpers: `GetFromJsonAsync<T>`, `PostAsJsonAsync`, `ReadFromJsonAsync<T>`. Check status codes and response bodies, just as a real caller would see them.
takeaways: WebApplicationFactory<Program> runs the real app in memory
CreateClient gives an HttpClient that goes through the full pipeline
ConfigureTestServices swaps real dependencies for fakes
Prefer a real database engine over EF Core's in-memory provider
pitfalls: Testing only handlers in isolation and missing binding, routing or JSON mistakes.

quiz.q: What does WebApplicationFactory.CreateClient() talk to?
options: A real Kestrel server on a random port
An in-memory TestServer running the app's full pipeline
A mock that returns 200 for everything
quiz.explain: Requests are processed in-memory by TestServer through the app's middleware and endpoints.

concepts.name: Authentication with JWT and cookies
concepts.summary: Identify callers with authentication schemes, check JWT bearer tokens, and read claims about the signed-in user.
concepts.why: Almost every API must know who is calling before deciding what they may do.
concepts.body:
Authentication answers "who is this?". In ASP.NET Core it is done by **authentication schemes** registered with `builder.Services.AddAuthentication(...)` and run by `app.UseAuthentication()` (added for you when authentication services are registered). A successful scheme produces a `ClaimsPrincipal` — the signed-in user — available as `HttpContext.User` or as a handler parameter.

Common schemes:

- **JWT bearer** (`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer`) for APIs. Callers send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, where the **token** — a string proving who they are — is a **JWT**: signed JSON saying who the user is and when that expires.
- With an **identity provider** — a service that signs users in for you, such as Entra ID, Auth0 or Keycloak — set `Authority` and `Audience`. The handler downloads the provider's signing keys and checks each token's signature, issuer, audience and expiry.

For websites whose pages are built on the server, the usual scheme is **cookies**: after sign-in the browser stores a small signed value and sends it with every request. It is usually combined with **OpenID Connect**, the standard behind "Sign in with Microsoft/Google" buttons, so users sign in through an external provider. When you want to store users and passwords yourself, use ASP.NET Core Identity and its ready-made endpoints (`MapIdentityApi`).

A **claim** is one statement about the user (`sub` for their id, `email`, `role`). Read them with `user.FindFirst("sub")?.Value` or `user.Identity?.Name`. Don't invent your own token formats or encryption.

Authentication alone blocks nothing: an anonymous request simply has an unauthenticated user. Blocking is the job of authorization (next lesson), which returns **401** (challenge: we don't know who you are) or **403** (forbid: we know, and you're not allowed).

For local development, `dotnet user-jwts create` issues test tokens that the JwtBearer handler accepts.
takeaways: Authentication schemes turn what the caller sends into a ClaimsPrincipal
JwtBearer checks a token's signature, issuer, audience and expiry
Use cookies + OpenID Connect for browser apps, bearer tokens for APIs
401 means not identified, 403 means not allowed
pitfalls: Turning off token checks (issuer, audience, lifetime) to 'make it work'.

quiz.q: An endpoint requires authorization and the request has no token. What status is returned?
quiz.explain: No authenticated user means the scheme issues a challenge, which is a 401.

concepts.name: Authorization policies
concepts.summary: Control access with RequireAuthorization, roles, claims-based policies and resource-based checks.
concepts.why: Clear, central access rules prevent the most damaging kind of API mistake: letting the wrong person do something.
concepts.body:
**Authorization** decides whether the authenticated user may perform an action. Apply it to endpoints with `.RequireAuthorization()` (minimal APIs), `[Authorize]` (controllers), or to whole route groups. `.AllowAnonymous()` / `[AllowAnonymous]` opt out.

**Authorization policies** name a set of requirements and keep rules in one place:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddAuthorizationBuilder()
    .AddPolicy("Admin", p => p.RequireRole("admin"))
    .AddPolicy("CanWrite", p => p.RequireClaim("scope", "todos.write"));
```

Use them with `.RequireAuthorization("CanWrite")`. Policy building blocks: `RequireAuthenticatedUser`, `RequireRole`, `RequireClaim`, `RequireAssertion(ctx => ...)` for a rule written as a lambda, and custom `IAuthorizationRequirement` + `AuthorizationHandler<T>` classes for rules that need services (database lookups, time of day).

Set a **fallback policy** (`SetFallbackPolicy(...RequireAuthenticatedUser()...)`) to make every endpoint require login unless it explicitly allows anonymous access; this is safer than remembering to protect each new endpoint.

**Resource-based authorization** handles "may this user edit *this* document?". Load the resource, then call `IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user, document, "CanEdit")` with a handler that compares e.g. the owner id to the user's id. Return `Forbid()` when it fails.

Test your access rules with integration tests, for both allowed and denied cases.
takeaways: RequireAuthorization / [Authorize] apply policies to endpoints and groups
Define named policies once with roles, claims or assertions
A fallback policy protects endpoints by default
Use IAuthorizationService for per-resource checks
pitfalls: Checking roles with if statements scattered across handlers instead of named policies.

quiz.q: What does a fallback policy requiring an authenticated user achieve?
options: Endpoints without explicit authorization metadata still require login
quiz.explain: The fallback applies whenever an endpoint specifies no authorization, making protection the default.

concepts.name: Background services
concepts.summary: Run long-lived work with BackgroundService, timers and in-app queues, using scoped services safely and stopping cleanly.
concepts.why: Job queues, scheduled tasks and cache warm-ups are part of most real services and must behave when the app shuts down.
concepts.body:
A **hosted service** runs alongside the web server for the app's whole lifetime. Derive from `BackgroundService` and implement `ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)`, then register it with `builder.Services.AddHostedService<T>()`.

```csharp
protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1));
    while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(ct)) { ... }
}
```

Key points:

- `stoppingToken` is cancelled when the app shuts down. Pass it to every await so shutdown is quick; the app waits up to `HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout` (30 seconds by default).
- Hosted services are **singletons**. To use scoped services like a `DbContext`, inject `IServiceScopeFactory` and create a scope per piece of work: `using var scope = factory.CreateScope();`.
- Catch and log exceptions inside the loop. Since .NET 6, an unhandled exception in `ExecuteAsync` stops the whole app by default (`BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior.StopHost`).
- `PeriodicTimer` never runs two ticks at once, unlike `System.Threading.Timer`.

For a work **queue** inside the app — a waiting line of jobs — register a `Channel<T>` as a singleton: endpoints write work items and return 202 Accepted, and the background service reads them.

Remember that an in-memory queue is lost when the app restarts. For jobs that must survive, use a **message broker** (a separate server that stores messages until they're processed) or a library such as Hangfire or Quartz.NET.

When several copies of the app run, every copy runs its hosted services, so a scheduled job may need a **distributed lock** to make sure only one copy runs it.
takeaways: BackgroundService.ExecuteAsync runs for the app's lifetime
Pass stoppingToken everywhere for a fast, clean shutdown
Create a scope per piece of work to use scoped services
Catch exceptions in the loop; unhandled ones stop the app
pitfalls: Injecting a DbContext directly into a hosted service's constructor (a captive dependency).

quiz.q: How should a BackgroundService use a scoped DbContext?
options: Create a scope with IServiceScopeFactory for each unit of work
quiz.explain: Hosted services are singletons, so scoped services must be resolved from a scope created per unit of work.

concepts.name: Route groups and endpoint filters
concepts.summary: Organize minimal APIs with MapGroup and add cross-cutting logic per endpoint with endpoint filters.
concepts.why: Groups and filters keep larger minimal API apps structured without repeating auth, prefixes and checks.
concepts.body:
**Route groups** share a prefix and conventions among endpoints:

```csharp
var todos = app.MapGroup("/api/todos").WithTags("Todos").RequireAuthorization();
todos.MapGet("/", GetAll);
todos.MapGet("/{id:int}", GetById);
```

Anything you can apply to one endpoint (authorization, **rate limits**, caching, OpenAPI details, filters) can be applied to a group, and groups can be nested. A common structure is one static class per feature with a `MapTodoEndpoints(this IEndpointRouteBuilder app)` extension method that creates the group, keeping `Program.cs` tiny.

**Endpoint filters** run around a minimal API handler, after binding, much like the filters controllers have:

```csharp
.AddEndpointFilter(async (ctx, next) => { /* before */ var result = await next(ctx); /* after */ return result; })
```

`ctx.Arguments` / `ctx.GetArgument<T>(index)` give access to the bound parameters, and `ctx.HttpContext` to everything else. Return a result early to skip the handler (for example a 400 for invalid input), or call `next` and change its result.

Filters vs middleware: middleware sees every request but knows nothing about the endpoint's parameters; filters run only for the endpoints they're attached to and see typed arguments. Use filters for argument validation, auditing specific operations or wrapping responses; use middleware for global concerns.

Filters added to a group run for all its endpoints, in the order they're added (outer first). Reusable filters implement `IEndpointFilter`.
takeaways: MapGroup shares prefixes and conventions (auth, tags, filters)
Organize features as extension methods that map their own group
Endpoint filters see bound arguments and can skip the handler
Use middleware for global concerns, filters for endpoint-specific ones

quiz.q: What can an endpoint filter do that middleware cannot easily do?
options: Access the handler's bound, typed arguments
quiz.explain: Filters run after parameter binding and get the handler's arguments through the context.

concepts.name: Caching and rate limiting
concepts.summary: Speed up and protect APIs with output caching, HybridCache and the built-in rate limiting middleware.
concepts.why: Caching makes responses faster and takes load off the database; rate limits protect your service from abuse and overload.
concepts.body:
**Output caching** stores whole responses on the server. Register `AddOutputCache()`, add `app.UseOutputCache()`, and mark endpoints with `.CacheOutput(p => p.Expire(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)))` or named policies. Keep separate copies per query string, header or route value, and **evict by tag** (`IOutputCacheStore.EvictByTagAsync("todos")`) when the data changes. By default only successful `GET`/`HEAD` responses to anonymous requests are cached.

**Data caching** caches values inside your code:

- `IMemoryCache`: kept in the app's memory — fast, but lost on restart and not shared between copies of the app.
- `IDistributedCache` (Redis, SQL Server): shared by all copies, but you convert values to bytes yourself.

`HybridCache` (`Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.Hybrid`, .NET 9+) combines a fast in-app layer with an optional shared one, and handles the conversion. It also prevents **cache stampedes**: when many requests miss the same key at once, the loading code runs only once and they all share the result: `await cache.GetOrCreateAsync(key, async ct => await LoadAsync(ct))`.

**Rate limiting** (`AddRateLimiter` + `app.UseRateLimiter()`) rejects excess requests — by default with 503, so set `RejectionStatusCode = 429` (Too Many Requests). Built-in limiters: fixed window (N requests per period), sliding window, `TokenBucketRateLimiter` (an allowance topped up at a steady rate) and concurrency (N at the same time).

Apply them with `.RequireRateLimiting("policy")`, and give each user or caller **IP address** its own limit (a partition), so one caller can't use up everyone's allowance.

In-app limits apply per copy of the app; with many copies behind a load balancer, also enforce overall limits at the front door, such as an API gateway.
takeaways: Output caching stores full responses; evict by tag when data changes
HybridCache adds two-level caching and stampede protection
Rate limiters reject excess load; set 429 as the status code
Give each user or IP address its own limit
pitfalls: Output-caching endpoints whose responses depend on the authenticated user.

quiz.q: What status does the rate limiting middleware return for rejected requests unless configured otherwise?
quiz.explain: The default RejectionStatusCode is 503, so most apps set it to 429 explicitly.

concepts.name: Kestrel, proxies and deployment
concepts.summary: Configure Kestrel's addresses, limits and HTTP versions, run behind reverse proxies with forwarded headers, and build container images.
concepts.why: Live incidents often come from hosting details: wrong caller IP addresses, endless HTTPS redirects, size limits and shutdowns.
concepts.body:
**Kestrel** is built on `System.IO.Pipelines` and handles many connections at once without a thread per connection. It supports HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (QUIC), plus **TLS** encryption. Configure it in code (`builder.WebHost.ConfigureKestrel`) or in settings under `Kestrel:Endpoints`; set addresses with `ASPNETCORE_URLS` or `ASPNETCORE_HTTP_PORTS` (official .NET container images default to port 8080).

Important **limits** (`KestrelServerLimits`): `MaxRequestBodySize` (about 28.6 MB by default), `MaxConcurrentConnections`, request header limits, `KeepAliveTimeout`, and minimum data rates that defend against callers who send data deliberately slowly.

Behind a reverse proxy or load balancer (Nginx, YARP, Azure Front Door, a Kubernetes ingress), the app sees the proxy's IP address and plain HTTP. Add the **forwarded headers** middleware early in the pipeline, so `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` update `RemoteIpAddress` and `Request.Scheme`. Only trust known proxies and networks (`KnownProxies`, `KnownIPNetworks`); otherwise callers can fake their IP. Without this middleware, `UseHttpsRedirection` can redirect forever, and generated links use `http`.

**Graceful shutdown**: when the platform asks the app to stop (on Linux, with the SIGTERM signal), ASP.NET Core stops accepting connections, lets in-flight requests finish and stops hosted services, all within `ShutdownTimeout`.

Make sure the grace period of your container platform — the **orchestrator**, such as Kubernetes — is longer, or the app is killed mid-shutdown.

**Containers**: `dotnet publish /t:PublishContainer` builds a **container image** without a Dockerfile, using the official base images, which run as a non-root user by default. "Chiseled" base images, stripped of everything but the essentials, are smaller and give attackers less to work with.
takeaways: Kestrel limits protect against oversized and slow requests
UseForwardedHeaders first, trusting only known proxy networks
Graceful shutdown lets requests finish within ShutdownTimeout
dotnet publish can build non-root container images directly
pitfalls: Trusting X-Forwarded-For from any source, letting clients fake their IP address.

quiz.q: Behind a TLS-terminating proxy, why does UseHttpsRedirection loop without forwarded headers?
options: The app sees every request as plain http and keeps redirecting
quiz.explain: Without X-Forwarded-Proto processing, Request.Scheme is http even for HTTPS clients.

concepts.name: Performance and Native AOT
concepts.summary: Make APIs fast and lean with async I/O, IHttpClientFactory, JSON source generation, CreateSlimBuilder and Native AOT.
concepts.why: Requests per second, memory use and startup time drive hosting costs and how fast the app feels to users.
concepts.body:
ASP.NET Core is among the fastest mainstream frameworks, so your own code usually decides the speed. The main levers:

**Never block on async code** (`.Result`, `.Wait()`, synchronous I/O). A thread stuck waiting can't serve anyone else; under load the thread pool runs out of free threads — **thread pool starvation** — and response times spike. That's why reading a request body synchronously is disallowed by default.

**Use IHttpClientFactory** (`AddHttpClient<T>`) for outgoing calls. It reuses connections safely, picks up address changes, and adds automatic retries and timeouts through `Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience` (`AddStandardResilienceHandler`).

**Stream large responses.** Return an `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`, which is sent as each item is produced, instead of building the whole list in memory first.

**Create fewer temporary objects** in code that runs on every request; measure with `dotnet-counters` (allocation rate, garbage collections, thread pool queue length) and `dotnet-trace`. And send big lists one page at a time and select only the columns you need: most "slow API" problems are database queries.

**Native AOT** compiles the app ahead of time into a single native program file: startup in tens of milliseconds and much lower memory use. That is great for **serverless** hosting (code started on demand by the cloud provider) and for packing many containers onto one machine.

It works for minimal APIs, gRPC and worker services, but not MVC or Razor pages. Start with `dotnet new webapiaot` or set `<PublishAot>true</PublishAot>`, use `WebApplication.CreateSlimBuilder` (fewer default features), and register a **JSON source-generated context**, so JSON conversion needs no reflection. The Request Delegate Generator turns your `Map*` handlers into compiled code automatically when AOT is on.

Fix every AOT and trimming warning: each one predicts a failure at runtime.
takeaways: Blocking on async code causes thread pool starvation under load
Use IHttpClientFactory and stream large responses
Native AOT works with minimal APIs: CreateSlimBuilder + JSON source generation
Treat trimming and AOT warnings as errors
pitfalls: Calling .Result on HttpClient calls inside a handler — it looks fine in tests and collapses under load.

quiz.q: Why does Native AOT need a JsonSerializerContext?
options: Reflection-based serialization isn't available, so serialization code must be generated at compile time
Because AOT apps can't return JSON otherwise at all, even with source generation
quiz.explain: Source-generated contexts provide the type metadata that reflection would otherwise discover at runtime.

concepts.name: Health checks and observability
concepts.summary: Expose health endpoints and instrument the app with OpenTelemetry traces, metrics and logs.
concepts.why: You can't run what you can't see: hosting platforms need health signals, and engineers need traces and metrics.
concepts.body:
**Health checks** tell load balancers and container platforms whether to send an app copy traffic. Register checks with `builder.Services.AddHealthChecks().AddCheck<DbCheck>("db", tags: ["ready"])` and expose them with `app.MapHealthChecks("/healthz")`.

Separate a **liveness check** (is the process responsive? keep it trivial) from a readiness check (can it serve traffic right now: database, other services), using tag filters. Then a database hiccup stops traffic for a moment instead of making Kubernetes restart every copy.

**Observability** — seeing inside a running system from the outside — is built on standard .NET classes:

- **Traces** via `System.Diagnostics.Activity`. ASP.NET Core, HttpClient and many libraries record an activity — a **span** — for each incoming and outgoing request, and pass the trace id on to other services in a W3C `traceparent` header. Create your own with an `ActivitySource`.
- **Metrics** via `System.Diagnostics.Metrics.Meter`: counters, histograms (how values are spread), up-down counters. ASP.NET Core publishes built-in ones such as `http.server.request.duration` and Kestrel connection counts.
- **Logs** via `ILogger`, tagged with the current trace id so you can find all logs for one request.

The **OpenTelemetry** .NET SDK (`OpenTelemetry.Extensions.Hosting`) collects all three and sends them over **OTLP** to monitoring services like Prometheus/Grafana, Jaeger, Azure Monitor or Datadog: `AddOpenTelemetry().WithTracing(...).WithMetrics(...).UseOtlpExporter()`. .NET Aspire sets this up by default.

For live diagnosis without redeploying, use `dotnet-counters monitor`, `dotnet-trace collect` and `dotnet-dump`. Keep the number of distinct tag values on metrics small: never tag with user ids or raw URLs, or the monitoring storage explodes.
takeaways: Separate liveness from readiness health checks
Traces use Activity/ActivitySource, metrics use Meter
OpenTelemetry collects traces, metrics and logs and sends them over OTLP
Keep the number of distinct metric tag values small
pitfalls: Making the liveness check depend on the database, so a database outage restarts every copy of the app.

quiz.q: Why should a liveness check usually not check the database?
options: A database outage would restart all healthy app copies without fixing anything
It is too slow to compile
quiz.explain: Liveness failures trigger restarts; dependency problems belong in readiness, which only stops traffic.
